title: Who to contact: banks, carriers, platforms, law enforcement
body_md:
## Route each problem to the team that can act

A single “cybercrime report” does not freeze a card, recover an account, or reverse a transfer. Match the contact to the thing at risk. Use a phone number printed on a card, a bookmarked app, or the organization's own website; numbers in suspicious messages and search advertisements can lead to impersonators.

**Money:** contact the sending bank, card issuer, or payment service immediately. State the payment method, time and whether you authorized it. Ask for a block, dispute, recall or recovery attempt appropriate to that method, plus a case number and written next steps. A transfer you approved under deception may be handled differently from an unauthorized withdrawal. Speed can matter, but no channel guarantees reimbursement. If the payment used a crypto exchange, report it to that exchange; do not send more crypto to a “recovery agent.”

**Phone number:** if service disappears or you see a port/SIM change you did not request, contact your carrier through its official support route and ask it to investigate, restore service and secure the account. Ask what account PIN or number-transfer protection the carrier offers. A legitimate outage also happens; use the carrier to establish the cause.

**Account:** use the provider's published hijacked-account flow. If a work account or device is involved, tell the employer's IT or security team promptly; their tools and reporting duties differ from a consumer's. Do not expect every platform to offer a live agent or instant restoration.

**Identity and reporting:** contact the creditor and the relevant credit-report service if a new account appears in your name. In the US, IdentityTheft.gov creates a tailored recovery plan, and IC3 accepts internet-crime complaints; keep your original evidence. In the UK, NCSC directs lost-money victims to their bank and to Report Fraud, or Police Scotland in Scotland. In Russia, the Bank of Russia describes a card-dispute path involving the bank and police; different transfer types require bank-specific instructions. Check your local official route elsewhere. If anyone is in immediate physical danger, contact local emergency services.

An authority's complaint feeds a record or investigation; it usually cannot perform the bank's account action. Keep a contact log with channel, date, case number, what was promised and when you will follow up. That makes the next call shorter and exposes conflicting instructions.

widget_config.goal: Route a money, carrier, platform, identity or police issue to the actor able to act, and keep a follow-up record.
widget_config.today_action: Save your bank's fraud contact, carrier support route and main account-recovery page from their official apps or websites in a private note.
widget_config.scope: Jurisdiction-specific reporting: US FTC/IC3, UK Report Fraud/Police Scotland, Russian Bank of Russia card route; other countries differ.

blocks.title: A fraudulent transfer and a fake hotline
blocks.situation: Synthetic: Elena sees a transfer she did not make. The alert text gives a “fraud desk” number; her card has a different number.
blocks.analysis: She uses the card or saved app, reports the transaction accurately, asks what can be stopped, and notes the case number. Calling the alert number could reveal more account data.

blocks.title: A real carrier outage
blocks.situation: Synthetic: Sam's phone has no service during a published local network outage. His carrier app shows no SIM or port change, and account logins are normal.
blocks.analysis: The symptoms resemble a SIM swap, but the carrier confirms a wider outage. Sam monitors the account rather than filing a false takeover claim or assuming the outage itself proves crime.

blocks.title: Who gets the first call?
blocks.setup: Synthetic: your number loses service; a payment app shows a transfer you approved after a fake invoice, and a social account is locked. Each decision below is an independent snapshot; no later prompt assumes that an earlier recommended action was taken.

steps.prompt: Where do you report the payment?

choices.text: The payment provider or sending bank via its official route, stating that you approved it after deception.
choices.consequence: They can assess any recall or dispute route.
choices.explanation: The payment service controls its own transaction process.

choices.text: Only the police, because the bank cannot help an approved transfer.
choices.consequence: A possible recovery route is delayed.
choices.explanation: The bank/provider still needs the report; outcome is uncertain.

steps.prompt: Separate snapshot: your number has lost service. What do you do about it?

choices.text: Call the carrier through a known number and ask about outage, SIM/port activity and account protection.
choices.consequence: You establish whether the number was moved.
choices.explanation: No service alone has several causes.

choices.text: Use the link in a new 'carrier security' SMS.
choices.consequence: The same number may be under attack.
choices.explanation: A text is not an independent route.

steps.prompt: Separate snapshot: your social account is locked. Which route handles it?

choices.text: Pay a recovery agent who promises access today.
choices.consequence: You may lose money and credentials again.
choices.explanation: Provider recovery is the authoritative route.

choices.text: Use the platform's published account-recovery procedure.
choices.consequence: The provider can verify ownership under its own rules.
choices.explanation: Restoration may take time or fail; avoid guarantees.

steps.prompt: Separate snapshot: you file a complaint with the US FBI’s IC3 about an online fraud. Bank/provider contact may still be outstanding. What should you expect?

choices.consequence: IC3 collects complaints; it does not operate the bank.
choices.explanation: IC3 does not operate the bank; contact the provider if you have not, or continue its case.

choices.text: Save the complaint and originals; contact the bank/provider through its official route if missed, or follow up on its existing case.
choices.consequence: The complaint is saved while you pursue or continue the payment report through the service.
choices.explanation: IC3 accepts complaints from affected people outside the US too, but it does not replace local reporting or bank action and does not promise status updates.

blocks.debrief: Different doors perform different actions. Recheck the route independently, state what happened accurately, and keep one log. Retry any missed step and replay.

questions.prompt: A card was used without your permission in Russia. Which is the correct first institutional contact?

choices.text: The issuing bank through the number on the card or its app.
choices.explanation: The Bank of Russia's card guidance starts with prompt bank notification and blocking.
It cannot block the card or start a dispute.

questions.prompt: A UK consumer lost money after account takeover. Which reporting pair matches NCSC guidance?

choices.text: Bank promptly, then Report Fraud or Police Scotland as applicable.
choices.explanation: The bank handles money; the local reporting route handles the crime report.
IC3 is a US system and does not replace the bank.

questions.prompt: A work mailbox is compromised. Who needs to know in addition to the provider?

choices.text: The organization's IT/security team via its incident procedure.
choices.explanation: They can contain connected systems and meet organizational duties.
They cannot manage the work environment.
